extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exercises for constructing, computing, and understanding fibered products (base change/pullbacks) of schemes; includes representable-functor viewpoint, practical algebraic calculations, and properties preserved under base change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of fibered products (glueing affines)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y is covered by affine open sets Yi and X and Z are affine (or more generally by gluing affines over overlaps), then the fibered product X ×_Z Y exists by constructing Wi = Xi ×_{Zi} Yi and gluing the Wi along the Wij; check the triple intersection cocycle condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify the universal property: construct maps γi on Vi = (β'')^{-1}(Yi), check they agree on overlaps Vij, and glue to a unique γ : V → W. Steps 1–5 outline doing the affine case, then covers of two, then arbitrary covers (glue via canonical open embeddings and cocycle conditions). Use Exercise 4.4.A to check cocycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal property is the criterion for fibered product
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate W for X ×_Z Y must satisfy the universal property: for any V with maps to X and Y commuting over Z, there is a unique map V → W making the diagram commute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In proofs and constructions always formulate and check this universal property (existence and uniqueness). Many arguments reduce to checking this on affine covers and glueing the unique local maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fibered product via representable functors
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement 'X ×_Z Y exists' is equivalent to 'h_X ×_{h_Z} h_Y is representable' where h_X denotes the functor Mor(-,X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate the construction of fibered products into the representable functor language: compute (h_X ×_{h_Z} h_Y)(W) = h_X(W) ×_{h_Z(W)} h_Y(W) (fibered product of sets) and then check representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability necessary condition: Zariski sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: If a functor is representable (by a scheme), then it must be a Zariski sheaf because morphisms to schemes glue on open covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely: for an open cover {Ui} of Y, the sequence h_X(Y) → ∏ h_X(Ui) ⇉ ∏ h_X(Ui ∩ Uj) is exact. Use this as a necessary condition when checking representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: h_X ×_{h_Z} h_Y is a Zariski sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: The fibered-product functor of representable functors, h_X ×_{h_Z} h_Y, satisfies the Zariski sheaf condition (Exercise 10.1.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use representability to prove this; check directly that elements glue on covers. This is a key step toward proving representability via local representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open subfunctors and representability of open embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: A subfunctor h' of h is an open subfunctor if for every map h_X → h the fibered product h_X ×_h h' is representable by some open subscheme U ⊂ X; in that case h' corresponds to an open embedding U → X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Cartesian square of functors to interpret open embeddings in the functor language; Exercises 10.1.D–F develop closure properties (intersection, subfunctor of subfunctor) and compatibility with open subschemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally representable Zariski sheaf ⇒ representable (Key Exercise 10.1.H)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a functor h is a Zariski sheaf and has an open cover by representable functors (i.e., is 'covered by schemes'), then h is representable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glue the schemes representing the open subfunctors using Exercise 4.4.A. This is the conceptual route used to prove existence of fibered products once local (affine) representability is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four atomic types of morphisms for computing base change
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four types of morphisms for which base change (fibered products) is particularly easy and from which general morphisms can be built: (1) base change by open embeddings, (2) adding a variable (polynomial extension), (3) closed embeddings (quotients), and (4) localization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use (1) to compute locally on source/target; use (2) and (3) to model arbitrary algebras as adding variables and imposing relations; use (4) to handle localizations/distinguished opens and generic points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change by open embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: Pullback along an open embedding Y ↪ Z is computed as the corresponding open subset of X; open embeddings are preserved by base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concretely, if Y ↪ Z is open and ψ: X → Z is any map, then ψ^{-1}(Y) ⊂ X satisfies the universal property of X ×_Z Y (see Exercise 8.1.D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adding variables corresponds to polynomial extension in tensor products
rubrics_metrics.description: A[t] ≅ A ⊗_B B[t] (Exercise 10.2.A), so forming affine space An over a scheme corresponds to base change by Spec Z[x1,...,xn].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to compute fibered products involving polynomial algebras; show universal properties for A[t] to prove the isomorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base change by closed embeddings / quotients
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y ↪ Z is a closed embedding defined by an ideal I, then the fibered product with a closed subscheme is a closed subscheme of the fibered product; closed embeddings are preserved by base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the ring level, extension of ideals and right-exactness of ⊗ produce the result (Exercises 10.2.B and following). Interpret intersections of closed subschemes as fibered products (Exercise 10.2.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization preserved by base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Base change with a localization S^{-1}B corresponds to localizing the fibered product: φ(S)^{-1}A ≅ A ⊗_B (S^{-1}B) (Exercise 10.2.G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This handles distinguished opens (B_f) and generic points (field of fractions) and is useful to compute fibers and local behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ring-theoretic computation of fibered products (tensor of quotients)
rubrics_metrics.description: If I ⊂ A[x1,...,xm] and J ⊂ A[y1,...,yn] are ideals, then A[x1,...,xm]/I ⊗_A A[y1,...,yn]/J ≅ A[x1,...,xm,y1,...,yn]/(I,J) (Exercise 10.2.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Exercises 10.2.A and 10.2.B to reduce to this calculation. Apply to compute explicit fibered products of affine schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of subschemes as fibered product
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection of two closed embeddings into X can be interpreted as their fibered product over X; similarly n-fold intersections of (locally) closed embeddings are fibered products (Exercise 10.2.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a scheme-theoretic notion of intersection compatible with base change and closed/locally-closed embeddings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback and scheme-theoretic fiber (definition and computation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π: Y → Z and ψ: X → Z, the pullback X ×_Z Y is the scheme-theoretic preimage of Y under ψ (the pulled-back family). The fiber of a morphism over a point p (with residue field K) is the base change to Spec K (scheme-theoretic preimage of the inclusion Spec K → Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute fibers in affine opens via localization and quotient: in an affine Spec A containing p, the map Spec K → Spec A is composition of localization and closed embedding, so use the four atomic base-change computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General fiber vs generic fiber; generically finite
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'general fiber' means fibers have a property over a dense open U ⊂ Y; 'generic fiber' refers to the fiber over the generic point (Y irreducible). A morphism π is generically finite if after base change to the generic point of each irreducible component, π becomes finite (or equivalently the preimage of the generic point is finite).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generic-finiteness can often be improved to finiteness over an open neighborhood under hypotheses (affine, finite type, locally Noetherian) — see Exercise 10.3.G and related hints using monic polynomials and denominators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finitely presented morphisms are locally pullbacks of finite-type maps to Noetherian schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Any finitely presented morphism Spec B → Spec Z can be presented locally as a pullback of a finitely presented morphism to some Spec Z[x1,...,xN] (Exercise 10.3.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use finite presentation to choose finitely many parameters for coefficients and express A as a quotient B[y1,...,yn]/(f1,...,fr); this allows transferring results from Noetherian base to locally finitely presented situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chevalley (constructibility) for locally finitely presented morphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a finitely presented B-algebra, then the image of Spec A → Spec B is a finite union of locally closed subsets; more generally, for a quasicompact locally finitely presented morphism π: X → Y with Y quasicompact, π(X) is a finite union of locally closed subsets (Exercise 10.3.I).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce to the affine finitely presented case using Exercise 10.3.H; this extends Chevalley's theorem beyond Noetherian hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Important monomorphisms: open, closed, localization
rubrics_metrics.description: Open embeddings, closed embeddings, and localizations of affine schemes are monomorphisms; monomorphisms are closed under composition, so compositions like locally closed embeddings are monomorphisms (Exercise 10.2.H).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these facts when reasoning about injectivity/uniqueness phenomena in base change and for identifying maps like Spec O_{X,p} → X as monomorphisms (but not necessarily open embeddings).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of properties preserved under base change
rubrics_metrics.description: Many 'reasonable' properties of morphisms are preserved under base change: (a) quasicompact, (b) affine morphism, (c) finite, (d) integral, (e) locally of finite type, (f) finite type, and (g) locally of finite presentation (Exercise 10.4.D and 10.4.E).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are typical closure properties used to check behavior after pulling back; use the four atomic computations and standard algebra to verify preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-finiteness and surjectivity preserved by base change (with caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quasi-finite morphisms (finite type + finite fibres) are preserved by base change (Exercise 10.4.F). Surjectivity is also preserved by base change (Exercise 10.4.G), though 'finite fibres' alone need not be preserved without further hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For quasi-finiteness, reduce to affine finite cases and use that finiteness is preserved by base change. For surjectivity, arguments may use field tensor nonvanishing and maximal ideal existence (Axiom of Choice) in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of fibers can reflect point-counting, nonreducedness, or field-extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature and 'size' of fibers varies: fibers over different base points can be multiple reduced points, nonreduced points, or single points corresponding to field extensions (Example 10.3.4 with y^2 = x over Q illustrating preimages of 1, 0, -1, and the generic point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a morphism, compute fibers via base change to residue fields or generic points to detect nonreduced structure, degree-of-extension phenomena, and to count points in several senses (points, vector-space dimension, field degree).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local computations (examples) guide intuition: C ⊗_R C and Galois phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit tensor-product computations (e.g., C ⊗_R C ≅ C × C or more generally L ⊗_K L ≅ ∏_{G} L for finite Galois L/K) show how fibered products reflect arithmetic/Galois structure and can produce multiple components corresponding to Galois group elements (Remarks and Exercises 10.2.3–10.2.4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such examples to anticipate nontrivial decompositions of fibered products and to understand how base extension can reveal symmetry or torsor structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up example as a base-change-friendly construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The blow-up Bl_{(0,0)} A^2_k can be realized as a closed subscheme of A^2_k × P^1_k cut out by xv = yu; its fiber over points of P^1_k is an isomorphism away from (0,0) and over (0,0) is an effective Cartier divisor (the exceptional divisor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete construction illustrates how fibers and base change describe geometric surgeries (blow-ups) and how exceptional divisors arise as fibers; compute fibers using the affine charts and the four atomic base-change tricks.
